curun.etymology: From curunã or Latin coronō. Compare Romanian cununa, cunun, încununa.

cãlcãnjiu.etymology: From Latin calcāneum. Compare Daco-Romanian călcâi.

cãloari.etymology: From Latin calōrem, accusative of calor.

cãrbunar.etymology: From Latin carbōnārius, equivalent to cãrbuni + -ar. Compare Daco-Romanian cărbunar.

cãtush.etymology: From Latin cattus, with a diminutive -ush added later.

dispartu.etymology: From Latin dispartiō. Compare Romanian despărți, despart.

ghios.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iōsum, from Classical Latin deorsum. Compare Romanian jos.

nsus.etymology: From Late Latin sūsum, from Latin sursūm. Compare Romanian sus, Sicilian nsusu, Catalan ensús.

firidã.etymology: From Greek θυρίδα (thyrída). Compare Bulgarian фирида (firida), Romanian firidă.

ncljis.etymology: Past participle of ncljid, perhaps corresponding to Latin inclūsus. Compare Romanian închis.

dishcljis.etymology: Past participle of dishcljid, perhaps corresponding to Latin disclūsus. Compare Romanian deschis.

glosses_en: past participle of dishcljid (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of dishcljis (feminine singular past passive participle of dishcljid used as an adjective)

pãrinti.etymology: From Latin parentem, accusative singular of parēns. Compare Romanian părinte.

dureari.etymology: From the verb dor, from Latin dolēre. Compare Romanian durere.

ndriptati.etymology: Probably from ndreptu/ãndreptu. Other theories have included a Vulgar Latin root *direct(it)ātem, from Latin directus, though this is unlikely. Compare Romanian dreptate.

ndriptedzu.etymology: From ndreptu, or from (ã)n- + Vulgar Latin root *dīrēctō, or from *indīrēctō, from Latin dīrēctus, with the Aromanian suffix -edzu.

glosses_en: used to form the first-person singular of some first-conjugation verbs
-edzu.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin -izō. Used as an infix in Aromanian verb conjugations. Compare Romanian -ez.

dultsi.etymology: From Latin dulcem. Compare Romanian dulce.

purtar.etymology: poartã + -ar, or possibly from Late Latin portārius, from Latin porta. Compare Romanian portar.

dzatsi.etymology: From Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥. Compare Romanian zece.

ndzeamin.etymology: From Latin ingeminō. Compare Romanian îngemăna, îngemăn, îngemănez.

sufrãmtseauã.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *subfronticella, from Latin sub + frontis + diminutive suffix -ella, possibly with influence from cilia. Compare (archaic) Daco-Romanian sufruncea. Some of the variant forms reflect confusion with or influence from sprindz

disuprã.etymology: From di + Latin supra. Compare Romanian deasupra; cf. also Dalmatian de zupra, Italian di sopra.

spãnac.etymology: Borrowed from Greek σπανάκι (spanáki), ultimately from Persian اسپناخ (espanâx).

pristi.etymology: From Latin per + super. Compare Romanian peste (archaic preste).

giurãmintu.etymology: From Latin iūrāmentum (“oath”), corresponding to giur + -mintu. Compare Romanian jurământ.

giurat.etymology: Inherited from Latin iūrātus. Compare Romanian jurat.

murtutsinã.etymology: From Latin morticīna, from morticīnus. Compare Romanian mortăciune.

moarti.etymology: From Latin mors, mortem. Compare Romanian moarte.

voauã.etymology: From Latin vōbīs, dative plural of tū. Compare Romanian vouă.

tinireatsã.etymology: tinir + -eatsã, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *teneritia, from Latin tener. Compare Romanian tinerețe.

flivar.etymology: From Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin (mensis) Februārius; possibly through the intermediate of Greek Φλεβάρης (Fleváris), or influenced by it later. Compare Romanian făurar.

mirindi.etymology: From Latin merenda. Compare Romanian merinde.

limnar.etymology: Either from lemnu + -ar or from Latin lignārius. Compare Daco-Romanian lemnar.

oauã.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *ōvāt, form of *ōvāre, from Latin ōvum. Compare Romanian oua, ouă.

floarã.etymology: From Latin flōs, flōrem. Compare Romanian floare.

strãveclju.etymology: strã- + veclju. Compare Romanian străvechi, Italian stravecchio.

tãciuni.etymology: From Latin tītiō. Compare Romanian tăciune.

tsitati.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”). Compare Romanian cetate.

foami.etymology: From Latin famēs. Compare Romanian foame.

grãditã.etymology: Probably related to Proto-Slavic *gordъ (“enclosure, fortification, town, city”). Compare Sardinian grad, Macedonian град (grad).

anumir.etymology: From Latin humerus, umerus, with the initial 'an-' added as a prefix later, or formed from un umir.

frãpsinet.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin fraxinētum, derived from Latin fraxinus (“ash tree”). Compare Romanian frăsinet.

pulbiri.etymology: From Latin pulvis, pulverem. Compare Daco-Romanian pulbere.

aratsi.etymology: From Latin recēns, probably reduced to a Vulgar Latin form *reces. Compare Romanian rece.

arcoari.etymology: Probably from aratsi + -oari. Compare Romanian răcoare. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *recor or from Latin rigor, rigorem, which had an attested use of "cold" (compare Sardinian arragore "frost").

arãtsescu.etymology: From aratsi. Compare Romanian răci, răcesc.

putoari.etymology: From Latin putor, putōrem. Compare Romanian putoare.

tilj.etymology: From Latin tilia, turned masculine in assimilation to other tree names, or through a Vulgar Latin root *tilius. Compare Romanian tei, Italian tiglio.

nfruntu.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *infrontō, from Latin frōns, or alternatively derived from frãmti, frunti. Compare Romanian înfrunta, înfrunt.

glosses_en: to leaf, leaf out, grow leaves or foliage
nfrãndzãscu.etymology: From frãndzã, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *infrondescō, from Latin frondescō. Compare Romanian înfrunzi, înfrunzesc.

carti.etymology: From Latin charta. Compare Romanian carte.

hãrtii.etymology: From Greek χαρτί (chartí), possibly partly through a South Slavic intermediate chartija (compare Bulgarian харти́я (hartíja), Macedonian хартија (hartija)). Compare Daco-Romanian hârtie. Cf. also carti, which as the same Ancient Greek root

acoalã.etymology: Borrowed from Greek κόλα (kóla), whence also Romanian coală.

cãrturar.etymology: From a derivative of carti, or from Late Latin chartularius, from chartula, ultimately from Latin charta. Compare Romanian cărturar.

nfoljiu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *infolliō, from Latin follis. Compare Romanian înfoia, înfoi.

ljepuri.etymology: Inherited from Latin leporem. Compare Romanian iepure.

fumealji.etymology: From Latin familia. Compare Daco-Romanian femeie (“wife”), Albanian fëmijë (“child”).

ndriptedz.etymology: From ndreptu, or from (ã)n- + Vulgar Latin root *dīrēctō, or from *indīrēctō, from Latin dīrēctus, with the Aromanian suffix -edz. Compare Romanian îndrepta, îndreptez.

mpruspitedz.etymology: From proaspit. Compare Romanian împrospăta, împrospătez.

ndzinucljedz.etymology: From dzinuclju, or from Vulgar Latin *ingenuclō < *ingenuculō, from Latin geniculum, with the Aromanian suffix -edz. Compare Romanian îngenunchea, îngenunchez.

nfãrtedz.etymology: Possibly from frati, or from a Latin verb fratrō, with the Aromanian suffix -edz and the prefix n-, ultimately from Latin frāter. Related to fãrtat.

nvicljedz.etymology: From veclju. Compare Italian invecchiare, Sicilian nvicchiari.

scãntiljedz.etymology: From scãntealji, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *scantiliō or *scintiliō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from Latin scintillō. Compare Romanian scânteia, scânteiez.

mpãricljedz.etymology: From pãreaclji. Compare Romanian împerechea, împerechez, Catalan emparellar, Spanish emparejar.

pluios.etymology: ploai + -os; possibly corresponds to Latin pluviōsus. Compare Romanian ploios.

pluinã.etymology: From ploai, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *pluvīna, from Latin pluvia.

frãn.etymology: From Latin frēnum. Compare Daco-Romanian frâu.

nfãrnu.etymology: From Latin īnfrēnō. Compare Romanian înfrâna, înfrânez.

furculitsã.etymology: Diminutive of furcã. Compare Romanian furculiță.

nfurcu.etymology: From furcã, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *infurcō, from Latin furca. Compare regional Daco-Romanian înfurci (variant înfurca).

pirunã.etymology: From Greek πηρούνι (piroúni). Compare Albanian pirun.

palmã.etymology: From Latin palma. Compare Romanian palmă.

hilji.etymology: From Latin fīlia. Compare Megleno-Romanian il'ă, Romanian fie.

nveastã.etymology: From Slavic nevĕsta, from Proto-Slavic *nevěsta. Compare to Daco-Romanian nevastă.

nfãrinedz.etymology: From fãrinã. Compare Romanian înfăina, înfăinez, Catalan enfarinar, French enfariner, Portuguese enfarinhar, Sicilian nfarinari, Spanish enharinar.

ghini.etymology: From Latin bene. Compare to Daco-Romanian bine.

nolgic.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin medius locus, following metathesis. Compare Romanian mijloc.

dizgiug.etymology: From diz- + giug or from a Vulgar Latin *disiugō, from Latin dis- + iugō. Compare Romanian dejuga, dejug and Italian disgiogare.

giuncã.etymology: From Latin juvenca, iuvenca. Compare Romanian juncă.

ghimtã.etymology: From Latin gentem, accusative of gens. Compare Romanian gintă, gint.

pitruniclji.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *peturnīcula. Compare Romanian potârniche.

pirdic.etymology: Probably from Greek πέρδικα (pérdika), from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix).

ljirtãciuni.etymology: ljertu, ljirtari + -ciuni, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *lībertātiō, *lībertātiōnem, from Latin lībertō. Compare Romanian iertăciune.

ljirtari.etymology: From ljertu or Latin lībertāre. Compare Romanian iertare.

ngrash.etymology: From gras or a Vulgar Latin root *ingrassiō, from grassus, from Latin crassus. Compare Romanian îngrășa, îngraș.

slãghescu.etymology: From slab or Serbo-Croatian slabiti. Compare Romanian slăbi, slăbesc.

vãrtos.etymology: From Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. Compare Romanian vârtos.

cadãr.etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قادر (kadir, kadır).

glosses_en: past participle of pot (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of putut (feminine singular past passive participle of pot used as an adjective)

silnãos.etymology: Related to silã. Compare Bulgarian and Macedonian силен (silen), Serbo-Croatian silan.

silã.etymology: From a Slavic language; ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sìla (“force, power, strength”). Compare Romanian silă, Bulgarian and Macedonian сила (sila), Serbo-Croatian sȉla.

glosses_en: to run or flow like a river
to fall like dewdrops, cover in dew
arãuredz.etymology: From arãu + the suffix -edz. Compare Romanian râura, râurez.

pãngãnãtati.etymology: From pãngãn + -ãtati, or possibly from Latin pāgānitās, pāgānitātem. Compare Romanian păgânătate.

cãcat.etymology: Past participle of the verb cac, corresponding to Latin cacātus. Compare Romanian căcat.

glosses_en: to make great efforts for, strive for
sprem.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *expremō, from Latin exprimō. Compare Romanian screme, screm.

griutati.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *grevitātem, from Latin gravitās, gravitātem. Or greu + -tati. Compare Romanian greutate.

heari.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n. Compare Romanian fiere.

njicuts.etymology: From njic + -uts. Compare Romanian micuț and Sicilian nicuzzu.

gãljinar.etymology: From gãljinã + -ar, or possibly Latin gallinārius. Compare Romanian găinar.

veardzã.etymology: From the plural of verdzu, corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *virdia, from Latin viridia, neuter plural of viridis (“green”). Compare Romanian varză.

glosses_en: pie filled with various vegetables or greenery such as cabbage
virdzari.etymology: From verdzu or veardzã, or less likely a Vulgar Latin root *virdiāria, from *virdia, from Latin viridia. Compare Romanian vărzare.

aroamig.etymology: From Latin rūmigō. Compare Romanian rumega, rumeg.

saltsi.etymology: From Latin salicem, accusative of salix. Compare Romanian salcie, variant salce.

scamã.etymology: From Latin squāma. Compare Romanian scamă.

scarmin.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *excarminō, from Latin ex- + carminō (“to card”), from carmen (“card for wool”). Compare Romanian scărmăna, scarmăn, Calabrese scarminare, Spanish escarmenar, Italian scarmigliare.

scarchin.etymology: From Latin scarpinō. Compare Daco-Romanian scărpina, scarpin.

glosses_en: to snatch, tear out, pull away
zmulgu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exmulgō, from Latin ex- + mulgeō. The alternative past participle derives from a Vulgar Latin root *exmulctus, from mulctus. Compare Romanian smulge, smulg.

lãptar.etymology: From lapti + -ar, or possibly from Latin lactārius. Compare Romanian lăptar.

lãptos.etymology: From lapti + -os, or possibly from Latin lactōsus. Compare Romanian lăptos.

alãptedz.etymology: Likely from Romanian alăpta (< French allaiter < Late Latin allactāre). By surface analysis, lapti + -edz.

eadirã.etymology: From Latin hedera. Compare Romanian iederă.

sturdzu.etymology: From Latin turdus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos. The initial s- possibly due to influence from sturnus, and the final -dz- perhaps because the word was reformed from the plural, or less likely through a Vulgar Latin *turdeus

strudz.etymology: From Latin turdus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos. The initial s- possibly due to influence from sturnus, and the final -dz perhaps because the word was reformed from the plural, or less likely through a Vulgar Latin *turdeus.

eapã.etymology: From Latin equa. Compare Romanian iapă.

suschir.etymology: From Latin suspīrāre. Compare Romanian suspina, suspin.

earbã.etymology: From Latin herba. Compare Romanian iarbă.

irbos.etymology: From earbã + -os, or from Latin herbōsus. Cognate with Sicilian irbusu.

earnã.etymology: From Late Latin hībernum, perhaps via the plural hīberna. Compare Romanian iarnă.

irnedz.etymology: From Latin hībernō, with the Aromanian suffix -edz. Compare Romanian ierna, iernez.

arnatic.etymology: From earnã + -tic. Possibly also linked to Vulgar Latin hibernaticum (attested in Medieval Latin), from Latin hibernum; compare Romanian iernatic. Cf. also French hivernage.

ahãntu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum tantum, from Latin eccum + tantum. Compare Romanian atât.

astrec.etymology: as- + trec. Cf. also the variant antrec, ntrec, with the prefix an- or n-, equivalent to Romanian întrece, întrec.

arushinã.etymology: From Latin rēsīna, from Ancient Greek ῥητῑ́νη (rhētī́nē). Compare Romanian rășină.

eascã.etymology: From Latin ēsca. Compare Romanian iască.

arãstornu.etymology: From arãs- + tornu. Compare Romanian răsturna, răstorn.

fugã.etymology: From Latin fuga. Compare Romanian fugă.

davan.etymology: Ultimately from Latin tabānus, through the intermediate of another language; compare Italian tafano, Venetan tavàn. Compare also the inherited form tãun, Romanian tăun.

tãun.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *tabōnem, or from Latin tabānus. Compare Romanian tăun. Cf. also the borrowed doublet davan, arriving through the intermediate of another language.

streclji.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *oestricula, derived from Latin oestrus. Compare Romanian streche.

mbãrbãtedz.etymology: From bãrbat. Compare Romanian îmbărbăta, îmbărbătez.

yitsã.etymology: From Vulgar Latin vītia, from Latin vītea, from vītis, vītem. Compare Romanian viță.

ayinji.etymology: From Latin vīnea. Compare Romanian vie.

yier.etymology: From ayinji, yinji, or from Latin vīneārius. Compare Romanian vier.

lacrimã.etymology: From Latin lācrima. Compare Daco-Romanian lacrimă.

lãcãrmos.etymology: From Latin lacrimōsus, equivalent to lacãrmã + -os. Compare Romanian lăcrimos.

lãcrimos.etymology: From Latin lacrimōsus, equivalent to lacrimã + -os.

lãcrimedz.etymology: From Latin lacrimō, with the Aromanian suffix -edz.

arãpescu.etymology: From arap + -escu. Compare archaic Romanian arăpesc.

lãrdzescu.etymology: From largu or Vulgar Latin *largiō, from Latin largior + escu. Compare Romanian lărgi, lărgesc.

ncred.etymology: n- + cred. Compare Romanian încrede, încred.

lishuredz.etymology: From lishor + -edz. Compare Romanian ușura, ușurez.

ljau.etymology: From Latin levō. Compare Romanian lua, iau.

ljinar.etymology: From ljin + -ar, or possibly from Latin līnārius. Compare Romanian inar.

amirã.etymology: Borrowed from Greek αμιράς (amirás), from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr) ~ آمِر (ʔāmir). Compare Ottoman Turkish آمر (amir).

dumnescu.etymology: From domnu. Compare Romanian domni, domnesc.

catargu.etymology: From Greek κατάρτι (katárti). Compare Romanian catarg.

varcã.etymology: Borrowed from Greek βάρκα (várka), from Late Latin barca. Cf. also Albanian varkë, Romanian barcă.

sãrbãturescu.etymology: From sãrbãtoari. Compare Romanian sărbători, sărbătoresc.

lupã.etymology: From Latin lupa, feminine of lupus.

ascapir.etymology: Uncertain. Compare Romanian scăpăra, scapăr. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *excapulō (compare Italian scapolare, Spanish escabullir) or from Latin ex + caperō.

licur.etymology: Related to licurici. Possibly ultimately linked to Latin lux, or alternatively of substratum origin.

lãngoari.etymology: From Latin languōrem, accusative singular of languor. Compare Romanian lingoare.

lãndzit.etymology: From Latin languidus. Compare Romanian lânced.

lãnar.etymology: From lãnã + -ar, or possibly from Late Latin lānārius, from Latin lāna. Compare Romanian lânar.

lãnos.etymology: lãnã + -os, or possibly from Latin lānōsus. Compare Romanian lânos.

dispolj.etymology: From Latin dēspoliō. Compare Romanian despuia, despui.

fatsiri.etymology: From fac, or from Latin facere. Compare Romanian facere.

melj.etymology: From Latin milium. Compare Romanian mei.

minutã.etymology: Ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin minūta, through the intermediate of another language. Cf. also Romanian minut.

minutedz.etymology: From minut, or less likely a Vulgar Latin *minutō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz). Compare regional/obsolete Romanian mănunta, Italian minutare, Portuguese miudar, Occitan menutar, amenudar.

suptsãri.etymology: From Latin subtīlis, subtīlem. Compare Daco-Romanian subțire.

muljari.etymology: From Latin mulierem. Compare Romanian muiere, Megleno-Romanian muľari, Istro-Romanian muľerĕ.

muljirescu.etymology: muljari + -escu. Compare popular or archaic Romanian muieresc.

ierm.etymology: From Latin vermis. Compare Romanian vierme, Sicilian vemmu, vermu, Venetan vermo.

mplinescu.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *impleniō (with the Aromanian suffix -escu), from Latin plenus (“full”). Compare Romanian împlini, împlinesc.

mpriunedz.etymology: From mpriunã with the suffix -edz. Compare Romanian împreuna, împreunez.

unescu.etymology: Inherited from Latin ūniō, with the Aromanian suffix -escu or through a late Vulgar Latin form *ūnēscō, as with many fourth conjugation verbs. Compare Romanian uni, unesc, Italian unire, unisco, Catalan unir, uneixo, French unir, unis.

disunescu.etymology: dis- + unescu. Compare Romanian dezuni, dezunesc.

dizlãchescu.etymology: diz- + alãchescu. Compare Romanian dezlipi, dezlipesc.

purumbu.etymology: From Latin palumbus. Compare Daco-Romanian porumb, porumbel.

culumbu.etymology: Ultimately from Latin columbus. Cf. Italian colombo.

purumbar.etymology: Probably from purumbu + -ar, or from Latin palumbārius. Compare Romanian porumbar.

pãrumbar.etymology: From pãrumbu + -ar, or from Latin palumbārius. Compare Romanian porumbar.

fãntãnar.etymology: fãntãnã + -ar. Compare Romanian fântânar, Spanish fontanero, French fontainier.

cãntãtor.etymology: Agent noun from cãntu + -ãtor, possibly corresponding to Latin cantator. Compare Romanian cântător, Italian cantatore.

mushconj.etymology: muscã + -onj, or derived from a Vulgar Latin root *musconea, from Latin musca. Compare Albanian mushkonjë.

amutsãscu.etymology: From mut or from Vulgar Latin ammutiō, ammutīre, with the Aromanian suffix -ãscu, or from Latin obmūtēscō. Alternatively from the variant form mutsãscu. Compare Romanian amuți, amuțesc, Italian ammutire, ammutisco.

glosses_en: to become mute, speechless; lose the ability to speak
mutsãscu.etymology: From mut or from Vulgar Latin *mutiō, mutīre, with the Aromanian suffix -ãscu, or from Latin mūtēscō (cf. obmūtēscō). Compare Romanian amuți, amuțesc (variant muți).

tushedzu.etymology: From tusi or from a change in conjugation of tushescu.

mãcari.etymology: From the verb mãc or Latin mandūcāre. Compare Romanian mâncare.

nãmalj.etymology: From Latin animālium (or animālia with a change of gender), from animal. Compare Romanian nămaie.

Sãrunã.etymology: Through a Vulgar Latin form (cf. Salonica, Greek Σαλονίκη (Saloníki)); ultimately from Ancient Greek Θεσσαλονίκη (Thessaloníkē).

didindi.etymology: di + dindi or Latin de deinde

ntardu.etymology: Possibly from Latin tarde, with the prefix n- and change of declension, or from the variant form tardu, influenced by ntãrdedz. Cognate with Sicilian tardu.

ditru.etymology: From Latin dē + inter. Compare Romanian dintru, din.

cãndilã.etymology: From Greek καντήλα (kantíla), κάνδηλα (kándila). Compare Romanian candelă, Serbo-Croatian kàndilo, Turkish kandil.

lundzimi.etymology: Frm lungu + -imi, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *longimen, from Latin longus. Compare Romanian lungime.

arburet.etymology: From Latin arborētum. By surface analysis, arburi + -et. Compare Romanian arboret.

cudalbã.etymology: From coadã albã, possibly representing a common Romance or Vulgar Latin formation; compare Romanian codalb, Sardinian codalbola.

cudubaturã.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *codabattula, from Latin coda < cauda (“tail”) + a derivative of battuō (“to beat”). Compare Romanian codobatură, Calabrese codivattula. See also similar formations in other Romance languages, with inverse order: Italian

nfoarfic.etymology: From n- + foarficã, or possibly from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin forficō (with the Aromaian prefix n- added), from Latin forfex. Compare Romanian forfeca, foarfec; cf. also Sardinian forfigare, Asturian aforfegar.

furtichedz.etymology: From foarticã, or possibly from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin forficō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from Latin forfex. Compare Romanian forfeca; cf. also Sardinian forfigare, Asturian aforfegar.

discalic.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *discaballicō, from dis- + Late Latin caballicō, from Latin caballus. Compare Romanian descăleca, descalec, Albanian shkalkoj.

cãlãriu.etymology: Related to cal. Cf. Late Latin caballarius, compare also Romanian călariu.

bitrãn.etymology: From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin vetrānus, syncopated form of Latin veterānus. Compare Romanian bătrân.

bishicã.etymology: From Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca. Compare Romanian bășică.

hivrescu.etymology: From heavrã, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *febrescō, from Latin febris.

doagã.etymology: From Latin doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ), from Proto-Indo-European *doḱ-éh₂. Compare Romanian doagă.

dugar.etymology: From doagã + -ar, or possibly Latin dogārius < doga. Compare Romanian dogar.

dinjic.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *dēmīcō, from Latin mīca. Compare Romanian dumica, dumic (earlier demica).

njauã.etymology: From Latin agnella. Compare Romanian mia, mială.

njioarã.etymology: Feminine form of njior, itself probably from njel + the diminutive -or, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *agnelliōlus (feminine *agnelliōla), from Latin agnellus, agnella. Compare Romanian mioară.

ntsingu.etymology: From n- + tsingu or possibly from Latin incingō. Compare Romanian încinge, încing.

cumnic.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin root *comminicō, from Latin communicō. Compare Romanian cumineca, cuminec.

nduplic.etymology: From n- + Latin duplicō. Compare Romanian îndupleca, înduplecare.

diplo.etymology: From Greek διπλός (diplós), from Ancient Greek διπλοῦς (diploûs).

alsivã.etymology: From Greek αλισίβα (alisíva) (as with Albanian alisivë), from Italian liscivia, from Latin lixiva. Compare Romanian leșie, which was inherited from Latin.

viglã.etymology: From (a)veglju; compare Romanian veghe. Cf. also Latin vigilia, Italian veglia, French veille.

marmurã.etymology: From Latin marmor, marmore, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble”). Compare Romanian marmură.

pãsturã.etymology: Probably from Latin pastūra, from pastus. Alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *pestula, diminutive of pestis. Compare Romanian păstură.

vinjiri.etymology: From Latin (diēs) Veneris. Compare Romanian vineri.

oasti.etymology: From Latin hostis, hostem. Compare Romanian oaste.

glosses_en: to cast an eye on something; aim
to cast a spell upon; fascinate
diucljedz.etymology: di- + ucljedz. Compare Romanian deochea, deochi; cf. also Calabrian aducchiare.

glosses_en: an eighth (one of eight equal parts of a whole)
top or highest point of (e.g. a head, tree, etc.)
creashtit.etymology: Most likely from crescu, creashtiri with the suffix -it. Less likely from creastã or a Vulgar Latin root *cristidum. Compare Romanian creștet.

shaptidzãts.etymology: shapti (“seven”) + plural of dzatsi (“ten”), literally "seven tens". Compare Romanian șaptezeci.

shapti.etymology: From Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Compare Romanian șapte.

glosses_en: peak, summit, top (of a mountain, tree, building, etc.)

culmã.etymology: From Latin culmen. Compare Romanian culme and Sicilian curma.

ciumã.etymology: Probably from Latin cyma, from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma). Compare meaning in Romanian ciumă (“plague, pestilence”), with meaning probably derived from the swellings caused by plague.

shasi.etymology: From Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. Compare Romanian șase.

amindoilji.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *amendoi, from Latin ambi dui, from Latin ambō (“both”) + dui, duae, from duo (“two”). Compare Romanian amândoi. Cf. also Old Italian amendue, Engadine amenduos, Old French andui, Occitan amdui.

biuturã.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bibitūra, from Latin bibitus, from bibō (“drink”). Compare Romanian băutură, Sardinian bibidura, bidura.

numescu.etymology: From numã. Compare Romanian numi, numesc.

glosses_en: straw (a dried stalk of a cereal plant)
palj.etymology: From Latin palea, made into a singular form, as with the Romanian equivalent pai, with the plural paie.

glosses_en: straw (a dried stalk of a cereal plant)
paljiu.etymology: From Latin palea, made into a singular form, as with the Romanian equivalent pai, with the plural paie.

pãljos.etymology: palj + -os. Compare Romanian păios, Italian paglioso, French pailleux, Catalan pallós, Occitan palhós, Spanish pajoso, Portuguese palhoso.

glosses_en: the object given as a pledge for a future marriage, such as a ring

njari.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n. Compare Romanian miere.

nuercu.etymology: Probably regressively derived from nuearcã as a masculine equivalent. Compare also Albanian njerk.

glosses_en: to drop, get rid of, throw away
aleapid.etymology: Probably from Latin lapidō (“to stone; throw stones”). Compare Romanian lepăda, lepăd.

peapini.etymology: From Latin pepō, peponem, through a Vulgar Latin root *pepinem. The Latin derives from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn). Compare Romanian pepene.

peashti.etymology: Inherited from Latin piscem. Compare Romanian pește.

glosses_en: fish shop; fishmonger's, fishmonger's shop, fishmarket

piscuescu.etymology: From pescu. Compare Romanian pescui, pescuiesc.

chirãmidã.etymology: From Greek κεραμίδι (keramídi). Compare also Romanian cărămidă, Megleno-Romanian chirămidă.

glosses_en: money amassed and put aside for old age
picunj.etymology: From Latin pecūnia. See also the near-synonym piculj, sometimes treated as a variant of this word.

glosses_en: money set aside as a reserve, or savings
piculj.etymology: Probably from Latin pecūlium. See also picunj, a near-synonym.

glosses_en: to delouse, look for and kill one's lice
dispiducljedz.etymology: From dis- + piduclju or piducljedz. Compare Romanian despăduchea, despăduchez.

glosses_en: past participle of pitrundu (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of pitrumtu (feminine singular past passive participle of pitrundu used as an adjective)

pitrumtu.etymology: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root pertūnctus (very rare term attested in a Late Latin work), as a variant participle of Latin pertundō, in place of the normal pertūsus. Compare Sardinian pertuntu.

arisescu.etymology: From Greek αρέσω (aréso), with the Aromanian suffix -escu.

plãtseari.etymology: From plac or from Latin placēre. Compare Romanian plăcere.

glosses_en: shady place where sheep rest during the hot hours of the day
to rest in a shady place during the hot hours of the day
amiridz.etymology: From the verb amiridz (see below), or from Latin merīdiēs (“noon, midday”); shift in meaning also found in Albanian dialect (Korça) mbriz (“midday nap for livestock”), standard mërzej (“to rest at noon (of animals)”). Compare Romanian meriz

plup.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ploppus, from classical Latin pōpulus. Compare Romanian plop.

glosses_en: orchard (land for cultivation of fruit or nut trees)
pumet.etymology: From Late Latin pomētum, from Latin pomus. Compare Romanian pomet, Italian pometo.

purcar.etymology: Probably from Late Latin porcārius, from Latin porcus. Compare Romanian porcar.

prumuvearã.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”), derived from Latin ver (“spring”). Compare Romanian primăvară, Albanian pranverë, Italian primavera.

pronj.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin root *purōnium, from Latin pus, puris. Compare Romanian puroi.

prunjedz.etymology: From pronj, pronjiu, with the suffix -edz. Compare Romanian puroia, puroiez.

chitros.etymology: cheatrã + -os or from Latin petrōsus. Compare Romanian pietros.

aryi.etymology: From Latin ārea. Compare Romanian arie.

pilicar.etymology: From Latin pollicāris, from pollex. Compare Romanian policar, which was probably borrowed, at least in its main form.

strãpungu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *extrāpungō, change of prefix from *trānspungō, from Latin pungō. Compare Romanian străpunge, străpung.

glosses_en: Romanian (of, from, or pertaining to Romania, the Romanian people or the Romanian language)
in the Romanian way or fashion

vlah.etymology: Borrowed from a surrounding language (compare Greek Βλάχος (Vláchos), Serbo-Croatian Vlah, Bulgarian влах (vlah), Old Church Slavonic влахъ (vlaxŭ)), from Proto-Slavic *volxъ, itself of Germanic origin, used as an exonym by other peoples fo

groapã.etymology: Probably a substratum word, akin to Albanian gropë, or possibly derived from it. Compare also Romanian groapă.

hãndac.etymology: From Ottoman Turkish خندق (hendek), from Arabic خَنْدَق (ḵandaq).

fusati.etymology: Ultimately from Latin fossātum; cf. Greek φουσσάτον (foussáton, “citadel”), Albanian fshat.

ngrop.etymology: From groapã. Compare Romanian îngropa, îngrop.

chimitir.etymology: From Greek κοιμητήριο (koimitírio). Ultimately from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion). Cf. also Romanian cimitir.

chimitiriu.etymology: From Greek κοιμητήριο (koimitírio). Ultimately from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion). Cf. also Romanian cimitir.

murmintedz.etymology: From murmintu. Compare Romanian înmormânta, înmormântez.

peaticã.etymology: Uncertain. Possibly linked to Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion) (cf. Latin pittacium (“label; patch”)), or from a Vulgar Latin root *piticus. Compare Romanian petic (“patch, rag, shred”), Calabrian pettica ("leather band, strip"); cf. als

arãm.etymology: Probably from Latin rimō. Compare Romanian râma, râm.

sapã.etymology: From Latin sappa. Compare Romanian sapă, Italian zappa.

astup.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *adstuppō < *stuppō, from Latin stuppa. Compare Romanian astupa, astup, Albanian shtupoj; compare also Sicilian stuppari, attuppari, Venetan stupar, Romansh stuppar, French étouper.

distup.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *dis-stupō, from Latin stuppa, or from dis- + [a]stup. Compare Romanian destupa, destup.

amurtsãscu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *admortēscō, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”). Compare Romanian amorțesc.

glosses_en: to lay waste, make like a desert, devastate

pustilii.etymology: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *pustyni, from *pustъ. Compare Romanian pustiu.

shcret.etymology: From Albanian shkretë, from Latin secretus. Compare also Romanian săcret, sharing the same Latin root as the Albanian word.

anyedz.etymology: From (ã)n- + yiu, or from yiedz, from Latin vivō (with a change in conjugation and the Aromanian suffix -edz). Less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *invivō, with a later suffix. Compare Romanian învia, înviez.

stranj.etymology: Uncertain, but probably of Slavic origin; compare Romanian strai (“clothing, garment”). Cf. Polish strój (“garment, clothing, attire”), Slovene srajca (“shirt”), Serbo-Croatian tranja (“rag, tatters”). Alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *ste

stranjiu.etymology: Uncertain, but probably of Slavic origin; compare Romanian strai (“clothing, garment”), which may or may not be the same word, but is likely related. Cf. Slovene srajca (“shirt”), Serbo-Croatian tranja (“rag, tatters”). Alternatively from a

glosses_en: clothing, garment, vestment, garb, dress, raiment
nviscãmindu.etymology: From Latin vestīmentum, with the prefix from Aromanian nvescu added. Compare Romanian veșmânt.

strãved.etymology: strã- + ved. Compare Romanian străvedea, străvăd, Italian stravedere.

videari.etymology: From ved or from Latin vidēre. Compare Romanian vedere.

glosses_en: past participle of ved (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of vidzut (feminine singular past passive participle of ved used as an adjective)

vidzut.etymology: Past participle of ved, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *vidūtus in place of Latin vīsus. Compare Romanian văzut, Italian veduto.

limpidzãscu.etymology: From limpid. Compare Romanian limpezi, limpezesc.

cãpestru.etymology: From Latin capistrum. Compare Romanian căpăstru.

ndzari.etymology: From n- + Slavic *zarja < Proto-Slavic *zorja. Compare Romanian zori.

glosses_en: at about 2 o'lock at night/in the morning
to see (far off in the distance)
ndzãrescu.etymology: From ndzari. Compare Romanian zări, zăresc.

glosses_en: past participle of apir (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of apirit (feminine singular past passive participle of apir used as an adjective)
past participle of crep (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of cripat (feminine singular past passive participle of crep used as an adjective)
cripatã.etymology: From the above past participle, with the meaning of the sun "breaking" or "cracking" through the horizon (cf. crack of dawn).

strãmut.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *extrāmūtō, in place of Latin trānsmūtō. Compare Romanian strămuta, strămut; cf. also Friulian stramudâ, Sardinian stramudai.

prãdãciuni.etymology: From Latin praedātiō, praedātiōnem. Compare Romanian prădăciune.

pljashcã.etymology: From a Slavic language; compare Serbo-Croatian pljačka, Bulgarian плячка (pljačka). Compare also Romanian pleașcă.

popã.etymology: Of Slavic origin, from Old Church Slavonic попъ (popŭ), from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas, “daddy, papa”). Compare Romanian popă. Less likely from a Latin popa, papa.

glosses_en: used to form a feminine noun equivalent, such as that of a profession, or the wife of a male with a certain profession (e.g. piscar (“fisher(man)”) + -oanji → piscãroanji (“woman that fishes or fisherman's wife”))
used to form the feminine of some animals, often with an augmentative effect (e.g. ursã (“bear”) + -oanji → ursoanji (“(large) she-bear”))
-oanji.etymology: From Latin -ōnea, -ōnia, feminine of -ōneus. Compare Romanian -oaie, also Albanian -onjë.

ursoanji.etymology: From ursã + -oanji. Compare regional or rare Romanian ursoaie (cf. ursoaică).

ursã.etymology: Inherited from Latin ursa (“she-bear”). For the prevalence of a feminine form compare Greek αρκούδα (arkoúda) and Macedonian мечка (mečka).

putridzãscu.etymology: From putrid. Compare Romanian putrezi, putrezesc.

pãduri.etymology: From Late Latin padūlem (“swamp”), from Latin palūdem via metathesis. Compare Romanian pădure.

pãduros.etymology: From pãduri + -os, or from Latin palūdōsus (through a metathesized Vulgar Latin form *padūlōsus). Compare Romanian păduros.

mpãdurescu.etymology: From pãduri. Compare Romanian împăduri, împăduresc.

plimunã.etymology: From Latin pulmōnem, accusative singular of pulmō (possibly through a metathesized Vulgar Latin intermediate *plumonem). Compare Romanian plămân, Sicilian primuni; also Greek πλεμόνι (plemóni).

pãni.etymology: From Latin pānis, pānem. Cognate with Romanian pâine.

dimineatsã.etymology: From di + Vulgar Latin *mānitia or from Late Latin dē māne + the Aromanian suffix -eatsã. Compare Romanian dimineață.

pãstalji.etymology: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pistālia, from Late Latin pistāre, from pinsō (“stamp, pound, crush”), or less likely a substratum term. Compare Albanian bishtajë, Romanian păstaie.

aroatã.etymology: From Latin rota. Compare Romanian roată, Occitan arròda.

arucutescu.etymology: From aroatã (variant forms arcoatã, arãcoatã, arocut, etc.)

nsãrtsinedz.etymology: From sartsinã. Compare Romanian însărcina, însarcinez.

mprumut.etymology: Presumably a deverbal of etymology 2. Compare Romanian împrumut.

brushtir.etymology: Uncertain; possibly from a Slavic *broštĭ. Compare Romanian brusture.

arushini.etymology: Uncertain. Compare Latin roseus. Probably from the verb arushinedz, itself from rushescu (“turn red, blush”), from arosh. Other explanations derive it from a Vulgar Latin root *rosinus ("rose-colored"), *russionem or *rosionem. May possibly

arushinedz.etymology: Either from arushini or from arushescu with the suffix -(in)edz. Compare Romanian rușina, rușinez.

arushescu.etymology: From arosh. Compare Romanian roși, roșire.

seati.etymology: From Latin sitis, sitem. Compare Romanian sete.

nsitedz.etymology: From seati. Compare Romanian înseta, însetez.

seatsiri.etymology: From Latin sicilem. Compare Romanian secere, seceră.

simnedz.etymology: From semnu. Compare Romanian semna, semnez.

glosses_en: to sparkle, flash, or strike down like lightning
sfuldzir.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fulger (with the Aromanian prefix s-, from ex-), from Latin fulgur. Compare Romanian fulger.

sfuldzirã.etymology: From the third-person singular present of sfuldzir or from Latin fulgurat through a Vulgar Latin *fulgerat or *exfulgerat. Compare Romanian fulgera, fulgeră, sfulgera, sfulgeră.

nshiuedz.etymology: From shauã, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *insellō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from Latin sella. Compare Romanian înșela, înșel, variant înșeua, înșeuez.

glosses_en: alternative form of nshiuedz- to saddle

shtiintsã.etymology: From Latin scientia, or shtiu + -intsã. Compare Romanian știință, also Albanian shkencë.

coaji.etymology: From Proto/Common Romanian, from South Slavic (compare Serbo-Croatian ко̏жа/kȍža, Bulgarian ко́жа (kóža)); cf. also Megleno-Romanian and Romanian coajă. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *koža.

glosses_en: fragment; strand of hair, blade of grass, etc.
shilji.etymology: Probably from Latin exilia < exilium, exsilium, likely deriving its meaning from "that which is exiled or removed from somewhere".

apalã.etymology: Compare Albanian pallë, Turkish pala, Romanian pală, paloș.

spumedz.etymology: From spumã or from Latin spūmō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz). Compare Romanian spuma, spumez, Italian spumare, spumeggiare.

strimburari.etymology: From Vulgar Latin root *stimulāria, from Latin stimulus. Compare Romanian strămurare, Megleno-Romanian strămulari.

glosses_en: each of the threads that make up the warp on a loom
ljitsã.etymology: From Latin licia, plural of licium. Compare Romanian iță.

distringu.etymology: dis- + stringu; cf. also Latin distringō.

disfac.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin disfaciō, from Latin dis- + faciō. Synchronically dis- + fac. Compare Romanian desface.

nidreptu.etymology: From ni- + dreptu. Compare Romanian nedrept.

shtirnutedz.etymology: From Latin sternūtō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz). Compare Romanian strănuta, strănut.

asurdzãscu.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin root *assurdiō (with the Aromanian suffix -ãscu), from Latin surdus or from obsurdēscō. Compare Romanian asurzi, asurzesc, Italian assordire, assordisco, French assourdir, assourdis.

Sãnmedru.etymology: From Latin Sanctus Demetrius, the meaning coming from the saint's holy day. Compare Romanian Sânmedru.

sãnãtati.etymology: From Latin sānitās, sānitātem. Compare Romanian sănătate, cf. also Albanian shëndet.

sãpuni.etymology: From Latin sāpōnem, accusative singular of sāpō, from Germanic. Less likely through the intermediate of Greek σαπούνι (sapoúni). Compare Romanian săpun, Sicilian sapuni.

sãpunos.etymology: From sãpuni + -os. Compare archaic Romanian săpunos.

agiun.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *aiūnō or *adiūnō, from Late Latin iēiūnō, from Latin iēiūnus. Compare Romanian ajuna, ajun, Spanish ayunar, French jeûner, Italian digiunare. Cf. also Albanian agjëroj, agjinoj.

talj.etymology: From Late Latin tāliō, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”). Compare Romanian tai.

taljiu.etymology: From Late Latin taliō, from Latin talea. Compare Romanian tăia, tai.

glosses_en: to pass or spend the autumn somewhere
ntumnedz.etymology: From toamnã. Compare Romanian tomna, tomnez.

nfarmãc.etymology: From fãrmac. Cf. also Romanian fermeca.

cutreambur.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *contremulō, from tremulō, from Latin tremulus, from tremō. Compare Romanian cutremura, cutremur.

trifolj.etymology: From Latin trifolium. Compare Romanian trifoi.

cutriyir.etymology: From Latin contribulō. Compare Romanian cutreiera, cutreier.

cãrari.etymology: From Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Compare Romanian cărare.

tupoarã.etymology: Borrowed from a Common Slavic toporŭ (Proto-Slavic *toporъ), ultimately of Iranian origin. Compare Romanian topor.

njurizmã.etymology: From Greek μύρισμα (mýrisma); compare Romanian mireasmă.

njurzescu.etymology: From Greek μυρώνω (myróno), with the Aromanian suffix -escu. Compare Romanian mirosi, mirosesc.

xihãsescu.etymology: From Greek ξεχνώ (xechnó), with the Aromanian suffix -escu, from Byzantine Greek ξεχάνω (xekhánō).

disumflu.etymology: dis- + umflu. Compare Romanian dezumfla, dezumflu.

glosses_en: to wave, move like a wave, undulate
undedz.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *undizō, from Latin unda. Derivable from undã + -edz. Compare Romanian undeza.

undos.etymology: undã + -os, or possibly from Latin undōsus. Compare archaic Romanian undos.

unglji.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ungla, from Latin ungula. Compare Romanian unghie.

yeaspi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *vespis, from Latin vespa, or perhaps formed from the plural of an earlier singular form. Compare Romanian viespe, Megleno-Romanian ghiaspi.

yispar.etymology: yeaspi + -ar, or from Late Latin vespārium (“wasp's nest”), from Latin vespa. Compare Romanian viespar, Italian vespaio, Sicilian visparu, Spanish avispero, Sardinian ghespàrju.

glosses_en: of or happening in the middle of summer

nviredz.etymology: From vearã. Compare popular or archaic Romanian văra, vărez (“spend the summer”).

nvireadzã.etymology: Conjugated form of nviredz, from vearã. Compare popular, regional, or archaic Romanian învăra, învărează (“to become summer”).

vishtidzãscu.etymology: From veashtid. Compare Romanian veșteji, veștejesc.

veduã.etymology: From the feminine of veduu, or from Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Latin vidua. Compare Romanian văduvă.

glosses_en: to become a widow or widower
nviduescu.etymology: From veduu, veduã. Compare Romanian văduvi, văduvesc.

vintur.etymology: From vimtu or from a Vulgar Latin *ventulō, from Latin ventilō. Compare Romanian vântura, vântur, Sardinian bentulare, vinturà.

vinturatic.etymology: From vintur, vimtu, with the suffix -atic.

glosses_en: to dry or air (e.g. clothes in the wind)
zvintu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exventō (“air out”), from Latin ventus (“wind”). Alternatively an independent formation. Cf. Romanian zvânta, zvânt.

glosses_en: holy herb, herb of the cross, vervain, verbena
yirghinã.etymology: From Latin verbēna. Compare Romanian verbină.

virghir.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin virgō. Compare Romanian vergură.

glosses_en: to make one lose his or her virginity; deflower

vitulj.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *vituleus, from Latin vitulus. Compare Romanian vătui.

glosses_en: little gate in a stable through which sheep are made to pass in order to be milked

plãtescu.etymology: From Proto-Slavic *platiti. Compare Romanian plăti, plătesc.

mpiltescu.etymology: From a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *plesti. Less likely to be tied to Latin implectō, from plectō. Compare Romanian împleti, împletesc.

glosses_en: Used with a stem to create a (usually abstract) noun relating to it; can be compared to -ship, -hood, -ness, -ity, etc.
-ilji.etymology: Probably from Latin -īlia, neuter plural of -īlis. Compare Romanian -ie.

glosses_en: -ness, -ity; used to form nouns from adjectives
roughly equivalent to -tion; used to form a noun when added to a verb root, describing that action or state related to the verb (also used with adjective roots sometimes)

striin.etymology: Ultimately from Latin extrāneus. Cf. Romanian străin.

glosses_en: wormy, containing or full of worms
yirminos.etymology: From Latin verminōsus. Compare Romanian viermănos.

lãmbric.etymology: From Latin lumbricus. Compare Romanian limbric.

ncljinãciuni.etymology: From Latin inclīnātiō, inclīnātiōnem. Compare Romanian închinăciune.

idul.etymology: From Greek είδωλο (eídolo). Compare Romanian idol, Macedonian идол (idol).

ntreg.etymology: From Latin integer, integrum. Compare Romanian întreg.

ntribari.etymology: From ntreb or from Latin interrogāre. Compare Romanian întrebare.

glosses_en: to be caught somewhere for the night, caught by nightfall
ntunic.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *intunicō, from Latin tunicō (“cover with a tunic”) from tunica. Compare Romanian întuneca, întunec.

ntunearic.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin tenebricus, and influenced by ntunic later. Compare Romanian întuneric.

glosses_en: to darken, grow obscure, dim; become cloudy
ãntunicã.etymology: Conjugated form of ãntunic. Compare Romanian întuneca, întunecă.

glosses_en: to darken, grow obscure, dim; become cloudy
ntunicã.etymology: Conjugated form of ntunic. Compare Romanian întuneca, întunecă.

niguredz.etymology: From negurã. Compare Romanian înnegura, înnegurez.

niguros.etymology: negurã + -os, less likely corresponding to Latin nebulōsus. Compare Romanian neguros.

gãrnuts.etymology: From the form grãnuts, from Vulgar Latin *granuceum or *granutium, from Latin grānum. Compare Romanian grăunte, grăunț.

tsir.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cibrum, from Latin cribrum. Compare Romanian ciur.

sitã.etymology: From a Slavic language (compare Bulgarian сито (sito), Serbo-Croatian and Polish sito), from Proto-Slavic *sito. Cf. also Romanian sită, Albanian sitë.

cãprinã.etymology: From Latin caprīna, feminine of caprīnus (“caprine”). The (Daco-) Romanian equivalent term is now lost, but an obsolete, regional, and popular term căprină was once attested to mean "a rugged sheep with long, uncurly hair and a rough temper

falcã.etymology: Ultimately from Latin falx, falcem (“sickle”), or through a Vulgar Latin form *falca; compare Romanian falcă; change in meaning, due to the shape of the mandible, also in Albanian felqinë (“jaw”). Compare also the semantic development of Sa

ayizmu.etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from Latin vindēmiō, but this presents phonetic difficulties and is unlikely. Other theories include a Greek origin. Cf. ayizmãciuni, ghismãciuni.

ayizmãciuni.etymology: The main root of the word (compare ghismã/yizmã) is of Greek origin. Corresponds to the archaic and regional Romanian iezmăciune (“November”), compare also izmă. See also ayizmu, ghizmedz.

cãrnar.etymology: From carni + -ar or from Latin carnārius.

aljurea.etymology: Probably from Latin aliubi, (a variant of alibi) + rē + a. Compare Romanian aiurea, French ailleurs.

glosses_en: to be delirious; talk nonsense, drivel
aljuredz.etymology: From aljurea + -edz. Compare Romanian aiura, aiurez.

aerã.etymology: This form probably from Greek αέρας (aéras) or perhaps Latin āēr, āerem; other variant forms more likely from Latin. Compare Romanian aer.

airisescu.etymology: From Greek αερίζω (aerízo). Compare Romanian aerisi, aerisesc.

glosses_en: to shave, barber, cut or clip hair
head of a leek, including its roots
bãrbutã.etymology: From barbã or possibly derived from a Vulgar Latin root *barbūtus, -a, from Latin barba (cf. Italian barbuto, French barbu, Spanish barbudo).

prash.etymology: Probably from Proto-Slavic *prazъ (compare Macedonian праз (praz), also Romanian praz).

disfingu.etymology: Related to or derived from asfingu (“raise dough”) (with the prefix dis-), itself from Latin fingō (“shape, fashion form, knead dough”), with a prefix added. Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin form *disfingō, disfingere.

glosses_en: past participle of disfingu (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of disfimtu (feminine singular past passive participle of disfingu used as an adjective)

disfimtu.etymology: Past participle of disfingu. Corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *finctus (instead of Latin fictus) with the prefix dis- (cf. Italian finto, French feint).

cãstãnji.etymology: From Latin castanea, from Ancient Greek καστάνεια (kastáneia).

cãshar.etymology: cash + -ar or possibly from Late Latin cāseārius, from Latin cāseus.

cãshari.etymology: Probably from Late Latin cāseāria, from cāseārius, from Latin cāseus.

cunj.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cuneus, possibly through the intermediate of another language. Compare Albanian kunj, Romanian cui.

cunã.etymology: From Latin cūna, singular of cūnae.

glosses_en: to rock or dandle a baby
leagãn.etymology: Either derived from the verb in the second etymology below, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *lecanis, from Ancient Greek λεκάνη (lekánē). Compare Romanian leagăn.

fucurinã.etymology: Related to foc, ultimately from Latin focus (“hearth”).

dizmal.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *dismallō, from Late Latin mallus (“lock of wool, flake”), from Ancient Greek μαλλός (mallós).

glosses_en: broad bean, horse bean, fava bean (Vicia faba)
fauã.etymology: From Latin faba. Cf. also archaic and dialectal Romanian făușel (“egg”), which may be from a related diminutive.

fuljinã.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *follinus, from Latin follis.

furnu.etymology: From Latin furnus. Cf. also Greek φούρνος (foúrnos).

glosses_en: to twitter or chirp in a deafening manner
gãrãescu.etymology: Either from Latin garriō, with Aromanian suffix -escu (compare Italian garrire, garrisco), or of onomatopoetic origin.

cãlugãr.etymology: From Greek καλόγερος (kalógeros). Compare Romanian călugăr.

ureaclji.etymology: Inherited from Latin ōricula, variant of auricula. Compare Romanian ureche.

gurnjescu.etymology: Probably from a derivative of Late Latin grunnium (“snout”) (cf. Latin grunniō, grunnīre (“grunt like a pig”)), with the Aromanian suffix -escu. Perhaps from the variant form grunjedz, grunjari, from a Vulgar Latin *gruniāre. Alternatively,

lãlãtoari.etymology: Probably from a variant form lãvrãtoari, ultimately from a derivative of Latin labōrō (“to work”) or Latin labōrātor. Cf. also Italian lavoratore.

lãvrãtoari.etymology: From a derivative of Latin labōrō (“to work”) (perhaps Vulgar Latin *laboratoria) or Latin labōrātor. Cf. also Italian lavoratore.

murnu.etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *morinus (“dark, tawny, swarthy, colored”).

oacljish.etymology: Possibly from oclju (“eye”), with the suffix -ish. Compare Romanian oacheș. See also calesh or calish, with senses closer to the Romanian word, referring to white sheep or goats with black spots on their heads.

ntric.etymology: Either a variant of nutric or mãtric. Likely from Latin nūtrīcō.

stãvrusescu.etymology: From Greek σταυρώνω (stavróno, “to crucify, to cross”).

astalj.etymology: as- + talj, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *extaliō, from Latin ex + taliō. Compare Italian stagliare, Sardinian stallai.

puduritsã.etymology: Probably derived from Latin pedūlis, with the Aromanian diminutive suffix -itsã.

arãzboi.etymology: From Proto-Slavic. Compare Serbo-Croatian razboj, Romanian război.

sãrcljedz.etymology: From Late Latin sarculō (+ the Aromanian suffix -edz), derived from Latin sarculum.

prãshescu.etymology: Derived from Proto-Slavic *poršiti. Compare Romanian prășesc.

plivescu.etymology: From Proto-Slavic *plěti, *plevǫ, *pleveši; compare Romanian plivi, plivesc.

glosses_en: place where a salt lick is located for sheep
sãrinji.etymology: From Latin salīna. Compare archaic and regional Romanian sănină, with the same meaning.

sprunã.etymology: From Latin prūna (“burning coal”), with an added prefix. Compare also Catalan espurna (“spark”).

spuzã.etymology: From Albanian shpuzë, from Latin spodium. Compare Romanian spuză.

stringlji.etymology: From stringu or possibly a Vulgar Latin *stringla < *stringula, from Latin stringō.

glosses_en: wool shorn close to the tail of the sheep
suelj.etymology: Derived from or related to suiljedz, or from a Vulgar Latin *sub īlium, from Latin īle, īlium (“lower abdomen, groin, flank”).

suiljedz.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *subīliō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from Latin sub + īlium (“lower abdomen below ribs; groin; flanks”) or īlia, from īle.

glosses_en: bundle of shorn wool that is longer and rougher, used for itches
sumã.etymology: From Latin summus (“highest, greatest”) or summa. Cf. Romanian sumă, with a different meaning and no longer a popular term.

sharã.etymology: Probably from Latin serra. Alternatively from Albanian sharrë, unless this word is instead derived from it. Compare Spanish sierra.

nsher.etymology: From n + sharã; possibly corresponds to Latin serrō, with a prefix added later.

vãnãt.etymology: From a derivative of Latin vānus; cf. also vānitās. Alternatively derived from Aromanian vãnãtati.

vãnãtati.etymology: vãnãt + -tati or possibly from Latin vānitas, vānitātem.

austru.etymology: From Latin auster, austrum (“the south wind”), with a change in meaning to the east wind. Compare Romanian austru, which has preserved the original meaning.

nordu.etymology: From French nord. Compare Romanian nord.

glosses_en: past participle of ascapit (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of ascãpitat (feminine singular past passive participle of ascapit used as an adjective)

carpin.etymology: From Latin carpinus. Compare Romanian carpen.

urghescu.etymology: From orbu. Compare Romanian orbi, orbesc.

mudzescu.etymology: From Latin mūgiō, with the Aromanian suffix -escu. Compare Romanian mugi, mugesc.

mudzit.etymology: mudzescu, mudziri + -it, or from Latin mūgītus (through a Vulgar Latin *mūgĭtus). Compare Romanian muget.

arujescu.etymology: From Latin rugiō, with the Aromanian suffix -escu. Compare archaic Romanian rugi, rugesc.

azgher.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exbēlō, from Late Latin bēlō, from Latin bālō, or alternatively from az- (from Latin ex-) + Vulgar Latin *verrō, from verres (“boar”). Compare (Daco-) Romanian zbiera, zbier, Megleno-Romanian zber, zberari.

amãreatsã.etymology: amar + -eatsã, or from Vulgar Latin *amāritia, from Latin amāritiēs. Compare rare or archaic Romanian amăreață, Italian amarezza.

glosses_en: to make heavy; make feel the weight, burden, weigh down
ngrec.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ingrevicō, a verb based on early Medieval Latin grevem, alteration of Latin gravem. Compare Romanian îngrec.

ngriunedz.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ingrevinō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from grevis, from Latin gravis. Compare Romanian îngreuna, îngreunez.

cleashti.etymology: From a Slavic form derived from Proto-Slavic *klěšča. Compare Romanian clește.

cheadin.etymology: From Vulgar Latin root *pedinus, from Latin pes, pedis. Compare Romanian piedin, Albanian pedim, Italian penero, pedano, pedene, Sicilian pèdinu, pèdanu.

pergurã.etymology: Ultimately from Latin pergula. Cf. Albanian pjergull, Italian pergola.

njadzã.etymology: From Latin media. Compare Romanian miază.

arãpãsedz.etymology: From Late Latin repausō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from Latin pausō. Compare Romanian răposa, răposez.

arãpas.etymology: From Late Latin repausō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from Latin pausō. Compare Romanian răposa, răposez.

purintu.etymology: Cf. purindã, purintã. Possibly ultimately derived from Latin polenta, but this is uncertain.

tramã.etymology: From Latin trāma. Cf. Romanian tramă, now used as a neologism.

trãmedz.etymology: From or related to tramã. Compare Italian tramare.

distrãmedz.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *distrāmō (with the Aromanian suffix -edz), from Latin trāma, or from dis- + tramã. Compare Romanian destrăma, destrămez.

leani.etymology: From Slavic lĕnĭ. Compare Romanian lene.

minutsalji.etymology: From minut or from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiālia, from Latin minūtia. Compare Italian minuzzaglia, Friulian minuçae, Old French menuisaille, Portuguese miuçalha. See also Romanian măruntaie and its cognates, from a different but related root.

glosses_en: small change, small things, things of little value, trifles
minutsami.etymology: From minut + -ami or from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiamen, from Latin minūtia. Compare Italian minuzzame, Friulian minuçam. Cf. also Romanian mărunțime.

cãtsãn.etymology: From Latin catīnum, from catīnus. Compare Romanian cățân.

cocã.etymology: From or cognate to Albanian kokë (“spherical object”). Perhaps ultimately from Latin coccum (“berry”), or Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed, kernel”).

shcljoapic.etymology: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *excloppitō or *excloppicō, from Late Latin excloppus, from cloppus. Compare Romanian șchiopăta, șchiopăt, cf. also Italian zoppicare.

shcljop.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *excloppus (compare Romanian șchiop, Albanian shqep, Occitan/Catalan esclop), from Late Latin cloppus (compare Old French clop, Italian zoppo).

aproapea.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ad prope, composed of ad (“to, at”) + prope (“near”). Compare Romanian aproape.

leadzi.etymology: From Latin lēgem, accusative singular of lēx, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s, from *leǵ- (“to gather”). Compare Romanian lege.

zãcon.etymology: Of Slavic origin, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *zakonъ; compare Bulgarian, Macedonian, and Serbo-Croatian закон.

ljei.etymology: Inherited from Latin illaei. Compare Romanian ei.

dãs.etymology: Compare Romanian dânsul; cf. also Old Italian desso.

noastrã.etymology: From Latin nostra(m). Compare Romanian noastră.

colj.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *[cōleum, cōlea] n, from Latin cōleus m, of Ancient Greek origin. Compare Romanian coi, coaie.

biutor.etymology: beau + -tor or from Latin bibitor, bibitōrem. Compare Romanian băutor.

adormu.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin addormiō. Compare Romanian adorm.

bãtalji.etymology: From Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō. Compare Romanian bătaie, with a different sense.

avinãtor.etymology: From Latin vēnātor; equivalent to avin + -tor. Compare Romanian vânător.

avinatic.etymology: avin + -atic, or possibly from Latin vēnāticus.

cinghine.etymology: Probably borrowed from Turkish Çingene, from Greek τσιγγάνος (tsingános). Compare also Romanian țigan.

ambrãtsitedz.etymology: From brats, with the prefix (a)m-, and the verbal suffix -edz. Compare Romanian îmbrățișa, îmbrățișez.

ascur.etymology: From Latin asper, asperum. Compare Romanian aspru.

asfingu.etymology: From Latin fingō (“shape, fashion form, knead dough”), with a prefix as- added, or through a Vulgar Latin form *exfingō.

spumig.etymology: From spumã, with an added suffix (possibly based on analogy with fumig), or less likely from a local Vulgar Latin *spumigō. Cognate with Romanian spumega, spumeg.

ared.etymology: From Latin rīdeō. Compare Daco-Romanian râde, râd.

carotsã.etymology: This form is borrowed from Italian carrozza. The native equivalent is cãrutsã (compare Romanian căruță).

caretã.etymology: Ultimately from Italian carretta. Cf. Romanian caretă, Bulgarian карета (kareta).

algheatsã.etymology: From albu + -eatsã, or from Vulgar Latin *albitia, from Latin albities, from Latin albus. Compare Romanian albeață.

ncãlduredz.etymology: From n- + cãldurã + -edz, or a variant of ncãluredz, influenced by cãldurã.

ascaldu.etymology: From Late Latin excaldō, from cal(i)dus (“hot”). Compare Romanian scălda, scald.

-eadzã.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin -izat. Doublet of -edzu. Compare Romanian -ează.

lãptucã.etymology: From Latin lactūca. Compare Romanian lăptucă.

tsilar.etymology: From Late Latin cellārium, from Latin cella. Compare Romanian celar. See also the synonym and doublet chilar, which came through Greek, ultimately from the same Latin route.

ascumsu.etymology: From Latin abscōnsus. Compare Romanian ascuns, Italian ascoso.

baltsu.etymology: From Latin balteus. Compare Romanian balț.

buyear.etymology: From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius or boārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius, boārius (“of cattle”), from bōs. Equivalent to bou + -ar. Compare Romanian boar, Sicilian vuiaru, Spanish boyero.

cãnichishti.etymology: cãnipã + -ishti. Possibly based on or adapted from Bulgarian konopište. Compare (Daco)-Romanian cânepiște.

discoapir.etymology: From Late Latin discoperiō < discooperiō, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. Compare Romanian descoperi, descopăr.

ncljei.etymology: From cljai, or from Vulgar Latin inclavō or *inclaviō, from Latin clāvus (“nail”) or clāvis (“key”) (or from Late Latin clavō with a prefix added). Compare Romanian încheia, închei.

deapir.etymology: From Latin dēpilō. Compare Romanian dăpăra, dapăr.

riniclju.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *reniclus, from contraction of Latin rēniculus (“little kidney”), from rēnēs (“kidneys”), from ren. Compare Romanian rinichi, Sardinian arrigu.

deapin.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *depānō or *depēnō, from Latin pānus, from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos). Compare Romanian depăna, depăn, Italian dipanare.

disfash.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin root *disfasciō or dis- + Late Latin fasciō, from Latin fascia. Compare Romanian desfășa, desfăș.

ditun.etymology: From Latin dētonō. Compare Romanian detuna, detun.

gljinduros.etymology: From gljindurã + -os, perhaps corresponding to Late Latin glandulōsus, from Latin glandula. Compare Romanian ghinduros.

mbuc.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *imbuccō, from Latin bucca. Compare Romanian îmbuca, îmbuc, Italian imboccare.

alavdã.etymology: From alavdu or possibly from Latin laudem, accusative of laus. Compare Romanian laudă.

lãndurã.etymology: From Latin lunter, luntrem, variant of linter. Compare Romanian luntre. Cf. also Albanian ljundrë, Dalmatian (Vegliot) lundro.

njilji.etymology: From Latin mīlia, plural of mīlle. Compare Romanian mie.

mushcljos.etymology: mushclju (“muscle”) + -os; may correspond to Vulgar Latin *musclōsus, from Latin musculōsus. Compare Romanian mușchios.

enurii.etymology: Borrowed from Greek ενορία (enoría). Compare Romanian enorie.

pupul.etymology: Variant of popul. From Latin populus.

mirindu.etymology: From mirindi, or possibly from Late Latin merendō, from Latin merenda. Compare rare/archaic Romanian merinda.

turturã.etymology: From Latin turtur, turturem. Compare regional Romanian turtură, Italian tortora.

turtureauã.etymology: From turturã + -eauã, or from Late Latin turturella, Latin turturilla, itself from turtur. Compare Romanian turturea, French tourterelle.

noadã.etymology: Several theories exist: from a Vulgar Latin root *nōda, resulting either from Latin nōdus crossed with or influenced by coadã in East Romance, or from Latin nates crossed with coda. Compare Romanian noadă (“coccyx”).

cãdzut.etymology: Past participle of cad. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *cadūtus, from Latin cadeō. Compare Romanian căzut.

glosses_en: past participle of cad (invariant form used with "to have" in verb constructions)
feminine singular of cãdzut (feminine singular past passive participle of cad used as an adjective)

ngiur.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iniuriō, from Latin iniūrior. Compare Romanian înjura, înjur, Megleno-Romanian ạnjur.

glosses_en: swear (on the Bible), take an oath
sprigiur.etymology: spri- + giur, or perhaps even from a Balkan Vulgar Latin construction composed of super or supra and iūrō, jūrō. Compare Megleno-Romanian sprijur, spridžur. No directly equivalent word was preserved in Daco-Romanian; however cf. the now arc

efharisto.etymology: Borrowed from Greek ευχαριστώ (efcharistó, “thank you, thanks”).

flitur.etymology: Uncertain, but cognate to Romanian flutura, flutur. Related to Albanian flutur and possibly derived from it. Other theories include a Vulgar Latin *flucturō, from Latin fluctuō, or *flutulō, or alternatively just an expressive creation of i

glosses_en: blister; cause or form blisters, break out with blisters
bishic.etymology: From bishicã or possibly Latin vēsīcō. Compare Romanian bășica, bășic.

muclji.etymology: Cognate to Romanian muchie. Either from a Vulgar Latin *mutlus, syncopated form of Latin mutulus, or from cumulus, with metathesis, and possibly influenced by mutulus.

cujuc.etymology: Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *kožuxъ. Compare Romanian cojoc.

glosses_en: to get a hunchback, bend one's back
gribuescu.etymology: Borrowed from South Slavic, compare Bulgarian се гъ́рбя (se gắrbja) and Macedonian се грби (se grbi, “to bend one's back, get a hunchback”), from Proto-Slavic *gъrbъ (“hump”).

limunadhã.etymology: Borrowed from Greek λεμονάδα (lemonáda), in northern dialects λιμουνάδα (limounáda). The later form with /d/ likely arose by influence of Romanian limonadă, Macedonian лимонада (limonada) and/or Albanian limonadë.

mulidi.etymology: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek μολύβι (molúbi), μολύβδι (molúbdi). Doublet of muliv.

muliv.etymology: Borrowed from Greek μολύβι (molývi). Doublet of mulidi /mulide.

tãvani.etymology: Borrowed from Greek ταβάνι (taváni), from Ottoman Turkish تاوان (tavan).

musahe.etymology: Perhaps akin to Greek μοσκιά (moskiá), μοσχιά (moschiá, “rose”).

arobul.etymology: Borrowed from Albanian rrobull (“pine; oak”), from Vulgar Latin robur (“oak”).

mãgulã.etymology: Uncertain. See Romanian măgură for more.

tsiva.etymology: From tsi + -va. Compare Romanian ceva, Megleno-Romanian tsiva, Istro-Romanian tsiva.

cantsiva.etymology: From the synonymous tsiva likely prefixed with can (“at least; nobody”), itself from Greek καν (kan), as a parallel formation of κάτι (káti), from καν (kan) + τι (ti, “something”), which also exhibits a stress shift to the initial syllable.

glosses_en: to set (of the sun, moon, stars, etc.)
surupseashte.etymology: Borrowed from Greek σουρουπώνει (souroupónei), itself from Aromanian soare apune (“sun sets”). Regularly borrowed via the simple past form, σουρούπωσε (souroúpose) → surupsi.

glosses_en: swelling (on the body); bump (on the head)
giumbã.etymology: Compare synonymous Bulgarian джумба (džumba), джумка (džumka), Macedonian џумка (džumka), Ottoman Turkish جومبه (cumba), Albanian xhungë, Greek τσούμπα (tsoúmpa), τζούμα (tzoúma).

giumcã.etymology: From the Slavic diminutive of giumbã, compare Bulgarian джумка (džumka) and Macedonian џумка (džumka), alongside Greek τσούκα (tsoúka, “bump on the head”).
